questions.prompt: Define thermal equilibrium.
questions.answer: The state in which two objects in thermal contact have the same temperature, so there is no net transfer of thermal energy between them.

questions.prompt: State the property of the thermodynamic (absolute) scale of temperature that makes it independent of any particular substance.
questions.answer: It does not depend on a physical property of any particular substance, such as its expansion.

questions.prompt: State the value of absolute zero in degrees Celsius.
State the equation relating temperature T in kelvin to temperature θ in degrees Celsius.
Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
State the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature and its symbol.
questions.answer: The kelvin (K).

questions.prompt: Describe the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles in a solid.
questions.answer: The particles are closely packed in a regular, ordered arrangement and vibrate about fixed positions.

questions.prompt: Describe the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles in a liquid.
questions.answer: The particles are close together but randomly arranged; they move about at random and can slide past one another.

questions.prompt: Describe the arrangement, spacing and motion of the particles in a gas.
questions.answer: The particles are far apart and randomly arranged; they move rapidly in random directions.

questions.prompt: Name the random motion of smoke particles suspended in air.
questions.answer: Brownian motion.

questions.prompt: Explain Brownian motion in terms of the kinetic model of matter.
questions.answer: The smoke particles are bombarded unevenly by much smaller air molecules moving rapidly at random, so the smoke particles move randomly.

questions.prompt: State what Brownian motion provides evidence for.
questions.answer: That the particles of a fluid are in continuous random motion.

title: Internal energy and change of phase

questions.prompt: Define the internal energy of a system.
questions.answer: The sum of the random distribution of kinetic and potential energies associated with the molecules of the system.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the internal energy of a body as its temperature rises.
questions.answer: The internal energy increases.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the internal energy of a substance during a change of phase.
questions.answer: The internal energy changes while the temperature remains constant.

questions.prompt: Explain why the temperature of a solid remains constant while it melts, even though energy is being supplied.
questions.answer: The energy supplied increases the potential energy of the molecules as bonds between them are broken; the average kinetic energy of the molecules does not change.

questions.prompt: State why 0 K is the lowest possible temperature.
questions.answer: It is the temperature at which a substance has minimum internal energy, so no more energy can be removed from it.

questions.prompt: State the effect of boiling a liquid at constant temperature on the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules.
questions.answer: The kinetic energy stays the same and the potential energy increases.

questions.prompt: Define specific heat capacity.
questions.answer: The energy required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (or 1 °C).

questions.prompt: State the equation linking energy supplied, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise.
questions.answer: E = mcΔθ, where Δθ is the temperature rise.

questions.prompt: State the unit of specific heat capacity.
questions.answer: J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Calculate the energy needed to raise the temperature of 2 kg of water by 10 K. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹.
State one way to reduce energy losses in an electrical experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block.
questions.answer: Insulate the block and use a lid, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: State the measurements needed to determine the specific heat capacity of a metal block by an electrical method.
questions.answer: The mass of the block, the temperature rise, and the current, potential difference and time for the heater.

questions.prompt: Define the specific latent heat of fusion of a substance.
questions.answer: The energy required to change 1 kg of the substance from solid to liquid at constant temperature.

questions.prompt: Define the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a substance.
questions.answer: The energy required to change 1 kg of the substance from liquid to gas at constant temperature.

questions.prompt: State the equation linking energy transferred and specific latent heat.
questions.answer: E = mL.

questions.prompt: State the unit of specific latent heat.
questions.answer: J kg⁻¹.

questions.prompt: Explain why energy must be supplied to melt a solid even though its temperature does not change.
questions.answer: The energy is used to overcome the attractive forces between the molecules, increasing their potential energy rather than their kinetic energy.

questions.prompt: Calculate the energy needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 °C. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹.
State the measurements needed to determine the specific latent heat of vaporisation of a liquid by an electrical method.
questions.answer: The mass of liquid that evaporates, the energy supplied by the heater (current, potential difference and time) and the constant temperature of the liquid.

title: Moles and the ideal gas equation

questions.prompt: Define one mole of a substance.
questions.answer: The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10²³ particles.

questions.prompt: State the value and unit of the Avogadro constant.
questions.answer: 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.

questions.prompt: State the equation of state for an ideal gas, identifying what n and T represent.
questions.answer: pV = nRT, where n is the number of moles and T is the thermodynamic temperature.

questions.prompt: State Boyle's law.
questions.answer: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, the pressure is inversely proportional to the volume (pV = constant).

questions.prompt: Explain how absolute zero is estimated from measurements of the pressure of a fixed volume of gas at different temperatures.
questions.answer: Plot pressure against temperature in °C; the points lie on a straight line. Extrapolate the line to zero pressure, and the intercept on the temperature axis gives absolute zero (about −273 °C).

questions.prompt: State the relationship between pressure and thermodynamic temperature for a fixed mass of gas at constant volume.
questions.answer: Pressure is directly proportional to thermodynamic temperature (p/T = constant).

questions.prompt: State the graph that should be plotted to verify Boyle's law for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
questions.answer: Plot pressure against 1/volume; a straight line through the origin shows that p ∝ 1/V.

questions.prompt: State two assumptions of the kinetic theory model of a gas.
questions.answer: Any two of: there are a large number of molecules in random, rapid motion; the molecules occupy negligible volume compared with the volume of the gas; all collisions are perfectly elastic; the time of a collision is negligible compared with the time between collisions; there are negligible forces between molecules except during collisions.

questions.prompt: State what is assumed about collisions between gas molecules in the kinetic theory model.
questions.answer: They are perfectly elastic, so kinetic energy is conserved.

questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of the kinetic model, how a gas exerts a pressure on the walls of its container.
questions.answer: Gas molecules collide with the walls and their momentum changes; each collision exerts a force on the wall, and many collisions per unit area give a steady pressure.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating pressure, volume and the mean square speed of the molecules of a gas.
questions.answer: pV = ⅓Nmc², where N is the number of molecules, m is the mass of one molecule and c² is the mean square speed.

questions.prompt: Explain why the pressure of a fixed volume of gas increases when its temperature increases.
questions.answer: The molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls more frequently and each collision causes a larger change of momentum, producing a greater force and hence a greater pressure.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the mean square speed of gas molecules.
questions.answer: The average of the squares of the speeds of all the molecules.

title: R.m.s. speed, the Boltzmann constant and internal energy

questions.prompt: Define the root mean square (r.m.s.) speed of gas molecules.
questions.answer: The square root of the mean of the squares of the speeds of the molecules.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating the Boltzmann constant k to the molar gas constant R and the Avogadro constant N_A.
questions.answer: k = R/N_A.

questions.prompt: State the equation relating the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule to thermodynamic temperature.
questions.answer: ½mc² = (3/2)kT, where c² is the mean square speed.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the internal energy of an ideal gas.
questions.answer: The sum of the kinetic energies of its molecules; there is no potential energy because there are no intermolecular forces.

questions.prompt: Describe the main features of the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution of molecular speeds.
questions.answer: It starts at the origin, rises to a peak at the most probable speed and has a long tail at high speeds; the area under the curve represents the total number of molecules.

questions.prompt: State the effect of increasing the temperature of a gas on its Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution.
questions.answer: The peak moves to a higher speed and becomes lower, and the curve becomes broader; the area under the curve stays the same.

questions.prompt: Define the radian.
questions.answer: The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius.

questions.prompt: Define the period of an object moving in a circle.
questions.answer: The time taken for one complete revolution.

questions.prompt: Define the frequency of an object moving in a circle.
questions.answer: The number of complete revolutions per unit time (per second).

questions.prompt: State the relationship between period T and frequency f.
State the equation for angular velocity in terms of period and frequency.
questions.answer: ω = 2π/T = 2πf.

questions.prompt: Calculate the angular velocity of an object moving in a circle with a period of 2 s.
questions.answer: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π ≈ 3.1 rad s⁻¹.

questions.prompt: State the direction of the resultant force on an object moving in a circle at constant speed.
questions.answer: Towards the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: Explain why an object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating.
questions.answer: Its speed is constant but its velocity is changing direction, so its velocity is changing.

questions.prompt: State the relationship between linear speed v, angular velocity ω and radius r.
questions.answer: v = ωr.

questions.prompt: State the two equations for centripetal acceleration.
questions.answer: a = v²/r and a = ω²r.

questions.prompt: State the direction of centripetal acceleration.
questions.answer: Towards the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: State what happens to the centripetal acceleration if the speed of an object is doubled while the radius is unchanged.
questions.answer: It becomes four times larger, because a ∝ v².

questions.prompt: Define centripetal force.
questions.answer: The resultant force acting on an object moving in a circular path, directed towards the centre of the circle.

questions.prompt: State the two equations for centripetal force.
questions.answer: F = mv²/r and F = mω²r.

questions.prompt: State what provides the centripetal force for a car turning on a level road.
questions.answer: Friction between the tyres and the road.

questions.prompt: State what provides the centripetal force for a satellite in orbit around the Earth.
questions.answer: The gravitational force between the satellite and the Earth.

questions.prompt: State what provides the centripetal force for a charged particle moving in a circular path in a magnetic field.
questions.answer: The magnetic force on the charged particle.

questions.prompt: Explain why the centripetal force does no work on an object moving at constant speed in a circle.
questions.answer: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so there is no displacement in the direction of the force; the kinetic energy of the object does not change.

questions.prompt: State the measurements needed to investigate circular motion using a whirling bung.
questions.answer: The mass of the bung, the radius of the circle, the tension in the string (from the hanging masses) and the time for several revolutions.

questions.prompt: Define simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: An oscillation in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the equilibrium position and is directed towards that position.

questions.prompt: State the defining equation for simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: a = −ω²x, where a and x are measured from the equilibrium position.

questions.prompt: Define the amplitude of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: The maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

questions.prompt: Define the period of an oscillation.
questions.answer: The time taken for one complete oscillation.

questions.prompt: Define phase difference.
questions.answer: The fraction of a cycle by which one oscillation leads or lags another, expressed as an angle.

questions.prompt: State the equation for angular frequency in terms of period and frequency.
questions.answer: ω = 2π/T = 2πf.

questions.prompt: State how the period of a simple pendulum can be measured accurately.
questions.answer: Time a large number of complete oscillations with a stopwatch and divide by the number of oscillations; repeat and average.

questions.prompt: State the general solutions for the displacement of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: x = A cos ωt or x = A sin ωt.

questions.prompt: State the equation for the velocity of a simple harmonic oscillator in terms of displacement.
questions.answer: v = ±ω√(A² − x²).

questions.prompt: State the maximum speed of a simple harmonic oscillator in terms of amplitude and angular frequency.
questions.answer: v_max = ωA.

questions.prompt: State where in its oscillation a simple harmonic oscillator has maximum speed.
questions.answer: At the equilibrium position (x = 0).

questions.prompt: State the velocity of a simple harmonic oscillator at its maximum displacement.
questions.answer: Zero.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by an isochronous oscillator.
questions.answer: An oscillator whose period is independent of its amplitude.

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of a displacement–time graph represents for an oscillator.
questions.answer: The velocity.

questions.prompt: State what the gradient of a velocity–time graph represents for an oscillator.
questions.answer: The acceleration.

questions.prompt: State what the area under a velocity–time graph represents for an oscillator.
questions.answer: The displacement.

questions.prompt: Describe the shape of a displacement–time graph for undamped simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: A sinusoidal curve (a sine or cosine curve).

questions.prompt: State the phase difference between the displacement and the acceleration of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: 180° (π radians); they are in antiphase.

questions.prompt: State the phase difference between the displacement and the velocity of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: 90° (π/2 radians); the velocity leads the displacement by a quarter of a cycle.

title: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator

questions.prompt: Describe how kinetic and potential energy interchange during simple harmonic motion.
questions.answer: Kinetic energy is maximum at the equilibrium position and zero at maximum displacement; potential energy is maximum at maximum displacement and zero at equilibrium. The total energy remains constant if the oscillation is undamped.

questions.prompt: State where the kinetic energy of a simple harmonic oscillator is maximum.
questions.answer: At the equilibrium position.

questions.prompt: State where the potential energy of a simple harmonic oscillator is maximum.
questions.answer: At the maximum displacement (the amplitude).

questions.prompt: State the equation for the total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: E = ½mω²A².

questions.prompt: State what happens to the total energy of a simple harmonic oscillator if its amplitude is doubled.
questions.answer: It becomes four times larger, because E ∝ A².

questions.prompt: Describe the shapes of the kinetic energy–displacement and potential energy–displacement graphs for a simple harmonic oscillator.
questions.answer: The kinetic energy graph is an inverted parabola, maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A. The potential energy graph is a parabola, minimum at x = 0 and maximum at x = ±A. The total energy is a horizontal straight line.

questions.prompt: Define a free oscillation.
questions.answer: An oscillation with no external periodic driving force, at the natural frequency of the system.

questions.prompt: Define a forced oscillation.
questions.answer: An oscillation produced by an external periodic driving force.

questions.prompt: Define damping.
questions.answer: The reduction in amplitude of an oscillation caused by energy being transferred to the surroundings by dissipative forces.

questions.prompt: State two effects of damping on an oscillating system.
questions.answer: The amplitude decreases over time, and the period increases slightly; the total energy of the oscillator decreases as energy is dissipated.

questions.prompt: Describe the difference between light damping and heavy damping.
questions.answer: With light damping the system oscillates with gradually decreasing amplitude; with heavy damping it returns slowly to equilibrium without oscillating.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by critical damping.
questions.answer: Damping that returns the system to its equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillating.

questions.prompt: Define the natural frequency of an oscillating system.
questions.answer: The frequency at which the system oscillates freely when it is displaced and released.

questions.prompt: Define resonance.
questions.answer: The increase in amplitude of a forced oscillation when the driving frequency is equal to the natural frequency of the system.

questions.prompt: State the condition for resonance to occur.
questions.answer: The driving frequency must equal the natural frequency of the oscillating system.

questions.prompt: Describe the amplitude–driving frequency graph for a forced oscillator.
questions.answer: The amplitude is maximum at the natural frequency and is smaller for driving frequencies above or below it, giving a peak.

questions.prompt: State the effect of increasing the damping on the resonance peak.
questions.answer: The peak becomes lower and broader, and occurs at a slightly lower frequency.

questions.prompt: Give one practical example of resonance and state whether it is useful or undesirable.
questions.answer: A radio receiver is tuned so that its resonant frequency matches the signal frequency, increasing the amplitude of that signal (useful).
